title: Legora CEO Max Junestrand on Legal AI and Building Globally (Pigment Perspectives)
author: Eléonore Crespo · Max Junestrand

dom.t: Legora expansion: Workflow usefulness must sustain global scale

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source predicts substantially broader agent execution of legal work, which is compatible with the cluster’s automation premise, but it does not address associate apprenticeship, expertise reproduction, verification competence, mentorship or reconstructed training. Its early-adoption thesis therefore provides insufficient evidence of a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: The shift from associates to partners using agents is meaningful, but the deeper transformation – legal work happening via agents as often as it happens via humans – is still ahead.

st.t: Legora partnerships: Adoption needs selected workflows and training
st.an: The source accepts that platform adoption depends on close vendor–firm collaboration and organisational change, while materially extending the proposition with a credibility-first market-entry model: partner with an anchor firm, validate use cases with lawyers, and pace releases around enterprise implementation timelines. It also offers reported commercial and partner-level adoption signals, but these do not independently prove accuracy or client outcomes.
qs: - Legora learned the motion of launching into new markets early and applied it repeatedly, from the Nordics to India to the US, always by partnering with the most credible firm in the market first.
Even if Legora could ship something in two weeks, the lawyers who actually use it need time to change the way they work.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Legora’s account aligns with the synthesis by treating newer language models as enabling previously impractical legal applications and by attributing adoption to close work with lawyers, security and compliance review, demonstrations, and successful use cases. It provides supportive commercial anecdotes but does not substantively address human verification, autonomous delivery, or whether specialist workflow layers will remain defensible as general models improve.
qs: There are so many solutions that will be rebuilt, so many new things that you can now go and solve, which were impossible with the technology pre-LLMs.” > > > > Max Junestrand,** Co-Founder and CEO, Legora  ## The first paying client was a friend's mom  Legora's first paying client found them at a party.
They passed security, compliance, and data privacy reviews, then brought the product directly to lawyers in the lunch canteen, asking them to input legal queries and see what came back.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s view that broader agent-mediated legal work is a future strategic direction rather than an established transformation. It does not, however, substantiate workflow integration, verification or how much lawyer supervision those agents will retain.
qs: The shift from associates to partners using agents is meaningful, but the deeper transformation – legal work happening via agents as often as it happens via humans – is still ahead.

st.t: Legora expansion: Workflow usefulness must sustain global scale
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by linking Legora’s international growth to useful first-use experiences, credible law-firm partnerships and improving model capabilities. Its commercial metrics and adoption anecdotes reinforce the expansion narrative, while its treatment of widespread agent-mediated work as still prospective aligns with the synthesis’s distinction between traction and measured legal-work improvement.
qs: When a few use cases worked well, interest spread quickly through the firm.
In less than two years, Legora has scaled from serving a single law firm in Stockholm to having clients in more than 40 markets.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that legal AI represents an early-stage transformation toward agent-mediated delivery rather than a completed market-wide shift. Its claim that early platform adopters may gain an advantage also aligns with competition moving toward differentiated delivery architectures, but this is a vendor-side strategic forecast rather than empirical evidence about bargaining shifts, returns or pricing.
qs: The shift from associates to partners using agents is meaningful, but the deeper transformation – legal work happening via agents as often as it happens via humans – is still ahead.
Legora's bet is that the firms that trust the platform now will be the ones best positioned when that shift arrives.

kp.k: Frontier models expanded the scope of solvable legal problems
kp.d: Junestrand attributes Legora's opportunity to access to GPT-3.5 in early 2023, following his co-founders' experiments with BERT-based legal AI since 2020. He argues that LLMs made previously infeasible solutions possible in detailed, high-stakes, document-heavy legal work.
qs: Everything changed when they got access to GPT-3.5 in early 2023.

What's interesting about the legal space is the green field. There are so many solutions that will be rebuilt, so many new things that you can now go and solve, which were impossible with the technology pre-LLMs.

kp.k: Application development took priority over owning the model layer
kp.d: The article contrasts early legal AI companies' 2023 investment in fine-tuning with Legora's strategy of using frontier models and concentrating on application functionality, including handling larger document collections and connecting to the web. Junestrand's rationale was that improvements in underlying models would improve the platform.
qs: But Legora made a different call: use every frontier model and build all functionality like boats. That way, when the tide rises, everything improves.
Rather than trying to own the model layer, Legora focused on the application. How do you work with a hundred documents, not just ten? How do you connect to the web?

kp.k: Later entry helped overcome distrust of early legal AI
kp.d: Junestrand claims lawyers' dissatisfaction with early-2023 AI tools enabled Legora to gain trust when it demonstrated a working product in mid-2024. This is his account of market reception, not a comparative performance evaluation. The article also reports a deliberate decision not to sell immediately after the Series A, prioritising product readiness.
qs: When a lawyer works with a tool, if it's not perfect, it's not good enough. A lot of people tried AI back in early 2023, and they hated it. When we came mid-2024 and showed them something that worked, we immediately got a lot more trust.
Legora also made a deliberate decision not to sell right after their Series A.

kp.k: Embedded law-firm collaboration supported product development and credibility
kp.d: The article describes Legora working inside Mannheimer Swartling, passing security, compliance and data privacy reviews, and demonstrating the product directly to lawyers. Successful use cases encouraged internal adoption, while the firm's endorsement helped attract other firms. This became the company's stated expansion model.
qs: They passed security, compliance, and data privacy reviews, then brought the product directly to lawyers in the lunch canteen, asking them to input legal queries and see what came back.
When a few use cases worked well, interest spread quickly through the firm.
That pattern – find the most credible partner in a new market, deliver for them, and let the market draw its own conclusions – became Legora's playbook for expansion.

kp.k: Partner use shifts delegation from associates toward agents
kp.d: The article describes associates primarily using Legora for speed, document checking and volume in 2025, followed by partners assigning tasks directly to agents rather than associates by 2026. It interprets this as a signal of trust and a move beyond individual augmentation. Its introductory takeaways date the shift to 2025, whereas the main account says by 2026; no staffing reduction or verification procedure is reported.
qs: In 2025, the primary users of Legora were associates – junior lawyers using the platform to work faster, get a second pair of eyes on documents, and handle volume.
By 2026, partners had started using it directly. Rather than delegating a task to an associate, they were giving it to an agent.
That shift happened at Legora's client firms in 2025.

kp.k: Client study reports additional discoveries using legal AI
kp.d: The article reports that a third-party study of Legora clients found 71% of platform-using lawyers surfaced material they otherwise would not have found, including precedents, clauses and data-room risks. It supplies no study name, sample size, methodology or date. Junestrand advances the separate normative claim that failing to use AI on a large transaction's data room is almost unethical; this is not presented as an adopted professional rule.
qs: A third-party study of Legora's clients found that 71% of lawyers using the platform surfaced things they otherwise would not have found, like relevant precedents, overlooked clauses, and risks buried in data rooms.
If you're working on a big transaction, it's almost unethical to not leverage AI in reviewing the data room, because the AI will find things that a human will not.

kp.k: Growth includes deeper adoption and adjacent professional workflows
kp.d: The article reports 300% net revenue retention in 2025 and attributes growth to deeper use within existing client firms and expansion into tax, compliance and risk, not just new customers. It also reports clients in more than 40 markets in less than two years and headcount growth from 40 to 400 in under 12 months. These are reported company growth figures rather than profession-wide adoption measures.
qs: In less than two years, Legora has scaled from serving a single law firm in Stockholm to having clients in more than 40 markets.
Their team grew from 40 to 400 people in under 12 months, achieving 300% net revenue retention in 2025.
It’s coming from deeper embedding in the firms they already serve and from expansion into adjacent areas including tax, compliance, and risk.

kp.k: Enterprise adoption constrains the pace of product rollout
kp.d: Legora plans quarterly product roadmaps despite being able to build faster, because enterprise clients need predictable implementation and adoption timelines. The article distinguishes technical delivery speed from the time lawyers require to change working practices.
qs: Legora plans product roadmaps on a quarterly basis, even though they can build faster than that.
Enterprise clients need to know where the product will be in three months so they can plan their own implementation and adoption timelines.
Even if Legora could ship something in two weeks, the lawyers who actually use it need time to change the way they work.

kp.k: Internal engineering agents accelerate development with human review
kp.d: The article describes an internal workflow that automatically triages Slack bug reports into Linear, uses Cursor to produce an initial pull request, and applies a security-review bot before human review. It reports little manual coding. Junestrand aims to extend engineering, product and design practices across functions through accessible central tooling, with individual curiosity driving uptake.
qs: The agentic tools Legora's engineering team uses internally have compressed their own build cycle dramatically.
Very little code is written manually.

His goal is to take the habits that engineering, product, and design (EPD) has built and make them accessible across the rest of the company by building a central tooling hub that curious people in any function can pick up and run with.

kp.k: International expansion combines local law with leading-firm partnerships
kp.d: Junestrand argues that individual European markets are too small for his growth ambition. Legora's expansion strategy integrates jurisdiction-specific case law, legislation and other legal sources, then partners with a prominent local firm. The article attributes relatively easy product internationalisation to similar legal technology stacks across markets, while identifying rapid multinational organisational growth as harder.
qs: First, the product needs to be integrated with local legal knowledge – case law, legislation, and other sources lawyers in that jurisdiction actually rely on.
Second, Legora looks for a winning brand to partner with.
The legal technology stack for large enterprises and law firms is remarkably similar across markets.
The harder part was internal, going from 40 to 400 people in under 12 months, across multiple time zones, while also keeping the organization coherent.

kp.k: Hiring prioritises demonstrated achievement, curiosity and ambition
kp.d: Junestrand's hiring framework for building the AI company emphasises exceptional prior achievement in any domain, curiosity demonstrated through independent exploration, and confidence that ambitious work is possible. These are his organisational recommendations, not findings about lawyer recruitment or professional training.
qs: Max looks for three qualities in candidates: a demonstrated history of doing something exceptional, genuine curiosity, and the mindset that you can “just do things.”
For curiosity, he asks candidates to tell him about the latest rabbit hole they went down, and to teach him something unusual.
Ambition can be found if you have a history of having done something exceptional. You need to have this innate want to be the best, to really push things to the limit.

kp.k: Agent parity with human legal work remains a forecast
kp.d: The article's conclusion distinguishes reported partner adoption from a future in which agents perform legal work as often as humans. It presents early platform trust as Legora's strategic bet on positioning client firms for that transition, without a timetable or supporting quantitative forecast.
qs: The shift from associates to partners using agents is meaningful, but the deeper transformation – legal work happening via agents as often as it happens via humans – is still ahead.
Legora's bet is that the firms that trust the platform now will be the ones best positioned when that shift arrives.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Junestrand describes AI moving from associate augmentation toward direct partner delegation to agents, improving discovery in legal documents and opening previously infeasible applications; the article predicts a broader agent-mediated transformation still ahead.
pts.d: Junestrand argues that LLMs make previously impossible legal applications buildable. He attributes Legora's adoption to arriving after early tools disappointed lawyers, with an application built to benefit from improving frontier models. The article describes associates using AI to work faster, review documents and handle volume, followed by partners assigning tasks directly to agents rather than associates; it interprets this as increased trust. Junestrand claims AI can identify issues humans miss in transaction data rooms and characterizes foregoing it as almost unethical, rather than citing an established professional obligation. The conclusion frames legal work being performed via agents as often as via humans as a future transformation and Legora's strategic bet, not an observed outcome. Junestrand also describes international expansion as facilitated by similar legal technology stacks, conditional on local legal-source integration and credible law-firm partnerships. Within Legora itself, the article reports compressed engineering cycles through agentic tooling and associates faster-moving teams with individual curiosity and accessible AI tools.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists principally of Junestrand's company experience, reported adoption and commercial metrics, and an unnamed third-party study of Legora clients.
pts.d: For improved discovery, the article cites a third-party study reporting that 71% of lawyers using Legora surfaced things they otherwise would not have found, including precedents, clauses and data-room risks. It supplies no study title, sample size, methods or comparison design. For adoption and trust, it offers Junestrand's account of disappointed early users, subsequent product demonstrations, and partners' direct use of agents. The Mannheimer Swartling account illustrates successful use cases spreading within a firm and a prestigious customer's role in attracting other firms. Reported commercial indicators include 300% net revenue retention in 2025 and clients in more than 40 markets; the article links growth to deeper embedding and expansion into tax, compliance and risk. These are presented as adoption and business indicators, not measured legal accuracy or productivity benchmarks. The internal engineering account describes automated triage, a first pull request, security review and subsequent human review, but provides no quantified build-time comparison. The future prevalence of agent-mediated legal work and the positioning advantage of early trust are strategic expectations without a quantified forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account locates the enabling model shift in early 2023, improved product reception in mid-2024, and partner-agent adoption around 2025–2026; the wider transformation has no specified deadline.
pts.d: The article attributes the initial technical opening to access to GPT-3.5 in early 2023 and contrasts early-2023 user disappointment with Legora's mid-2024 reception. Its chronology of partner adoption is not fully consistent: the key takeaways place the shift in 2025, while the main text says associates were the primary users in 2025 and partners had begun direct use by 2026. The conclusion provides no date for agents mediating legal work as often as humans. Enterprise adoption is qualified by implementation planning and the time lawyers need to change workflows, leading Legora to use quarterly roadmaps despite faster development capability. International expansion requires integration with jurisdiction-specific case law, legislation and other sources, together with a credible local partner. The transactional-review claim specifically concerns large transactions and data rooms, rather than every legal task.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The account primarily concerns associates, partners and enterprise law-firm customers, with adjacent effects on tax, compliance and risk users and on Legora's own workforce.
pts.d: Associates are described as gaining speed, document-review assistance and capacity for volume. Partners gain the ability to delegate directly to agents, potentially redirecting tasks that otherwise would go to associates; the source does not quantify employment losses or changes to staffing ratios. Transaction lawyers are said to gain additional issue detection in data rooms. Law firms and large enterprise customers face workflow-change and implementation demands, while the article suggests firms trusting the platform now will be better positioned for future agent adoption. Firms in new jurisdictions gain access through localization and flagship partnerships. Tax, compliance and risk are identified as adjacent expansion areas without detailed role-level outcomes. Legora is the software provider, not an alternative legal service provider delivering the underlying legal work. Its engineering staff reportedly do less manual coding, and the CEO seeks to extend AI-enabled working habits across functions. The document does not make concrete claims about individual clients' access to justice, legal fees or public-facing service outcomes.
